pages.title: Course home
pages.text: Build a robot, drive it, and see what it sees # Start with a cube and four wheels. Add physics, take control with your keyboard, and watch lidar measurements arrive in ROS 2. Then import Carter, generate labelled warehouse images, and connect simulated sensors to robot software. This hands-on course adapts NVIDIA's Getting Started With Isaac Sim learning path to Isaac Sim 6.1.0-rc.26 . It contains 12 practical lessons and an optional hardware-in-the-loop module . Each practical lesson has a short narrated video, guided steps, exercises, and a result to check. Read it online: saeedahmadicp.github.io/isaac-sim-6-getting-started · Source: github.com/saeedahmadicp/isaac-sim-6-getting-started Build your first robot → Check what you need Build this in Module 1. Actual Isaac Sim 6.1 capture; camera, lights, and colours adjusted for clarity. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 2 min · download .mp4 Before you start # You should be comfortable opening a terminal and navigating files. Module 1 introduces the simulator from scratch; you do not need to know the names of its panels or physics components yet. Later lessons use ROS 2 commands and Python. You need When you need it A working Isaac Sim installation and compatible NVIDIA GPU Before lesson 1.1; launch the app and open a blank scene Internet access for NVIDIA robot and environment assets When loading remote assets; the first load can take longer ROS 2 command-line tools and RViz Before lesson 1.4; follow Set up ROS 2 Jazzy A Python background Helpful for the synthetic-data and scripting lessons Isaac ROS container setup For the external perception continuation after lesson 4.3 A Jetson Only for the optional hardware exercise in Module 5 The reference setup is Ubuntu 24.04, Isaac Sim 6.1.0-rc.26, and ROS 2 Jazzy. Check your version with cat VERSION from the Isaac Sim installation folder. If you are following NVIDIA's older videos, keep the 4.5 → 6.1 guide nearby; the blue change notes explain differences at the steps where they matter. Get the course files # The checkpoint scripts expect this course to sit in a learning_resource/ folder inside your Isaac Sim installation , next to isaac-sim.sh and python.sh : cd ~/isaacsim # your Isaac Sim installation folder git clone https://github.com/saeedahmadicp/isaac-sim-6-getting-started.git learning_resource python3 learning_resource/site/serve.py # optional: browse the course at http://127.0.0.1:8765/site/ Choose your next result # Module What you will make Start here 1 · Your first robot A robot built from shapes, driven by keyboard, with a lidar feed in ROS 2 Build, drive, and sense 2 · Work with robot assets A drivable Carter imported from URDF, then a comparison with Nova Carter Import Carter 3 · Perception data A small randomized pallet-jack dataset whose images and labels you can inspect Generate and inspect data 4 · Connect robot software ROS 2 motion commands, Python scenes, and camera images for a perception pipeline Connect the control loop 5 · Optional hardware extension A plan and connection checks for moving robot software to a Jetson Explore hardware-in-the-loop New to simulation? Follow Modules 1 and 2 first. Module 3 is a perception-data branch; it is not a prerequisite for the ROS 2 control lessons in Module 4. Module 5 requires additional hardware for the full exercise, but includes a same-PC clock exercise. Learn by predicting, trying, and checking # See the destination. Read the lesson goal and watch the short overview. The video introduces the workflow; use the written steps for the hands-on work. Make a prediction. Before changing a drive, joint, or sensor setting, decide what you expect to happen. Write down a speed, direction, or visible change. Try one change. Run the scene and compare the result with your prediction. Unexpected motion is useful evidence: use the troubleshooting table to narrow down the cause. Keep your result. Save the scene and complete the checks before moving on. The final exercise asks you to change something without following every click again. Lesson 1.1 is estimated at 45–60 minutes. Later pages show their own hands-on estimates; allow extra time for installation, asset downloads, and shader compilation. When you get stuck # Several lessons have checkpoint scripts that build a reference scene or test an output. Compare the reference with your work: which joint, setting, or graph connection differs? Some lessons share a script; camera/container and hardware exercises still need manual checks. Run commands from your Isaac Sim installation folder: ./isaac-sim.sh # In a separate terminal, after closing the GUI if GPU memory is limited: ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m1_build_simple_robot.py --headless --test A checkpoint tests the behavior described on its lesson page. It does not replace the manual GUI, keyboard, RViz, container, and hardware exercises. Course files and local website # The Markdown lessons are the editable source. The website instructions explain how to serve the course and rebuild it after an edit. Videos, diagrams, checkpoint scripts, and generated scenes live in the sibling videos/ , diagrams/ , scripts/ , and output/ folders. Keep your own scene filenames separate from checkpoint outputs so you can compare them later. Credits and notices # This is an unofficial, community adaptation of NVIDIA's free Getting Started With Isaac Sim learning path. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NVIDIA. NVIDIA, Isaac Sim, Omniverse, Jetson and related names are trademarks of NVIDIA Corporation. scripts/m3_palletjack_sdg.py is ported from NVIDIA-AI-IOT/synthetic_data_generation_training_workflow (MIT License, © 2022 NVIDIA Corporation); its header keeps that notice. The Carter URDF and meshes used in Module 2 belong to Isaac Sim and are not included here; lesson 2.1 copies them from your own installation. Robot, environment and prop assets are streamed from NVIDIA's asset server at run time under Isaac Sim's own license terms. Narration in the videos was generated with ElevenLabs; diagrams were drawn for this course.

pages.title: Set up ROS 2 Jazzy
pages.text: One-time setup: ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04 # Isaac Sim does not need this. 6.1 ships its own ROS 2 Jazzy libraries ( exts/isaacsim.ros2.core/jazzy ) and loads them automatically. Install system ROS 2 only for the tools you run outside Isaac Sim, which the course uses in lessons 1.4, 4.1 and 4.3: ros2 topic list / echo / pub rviz2 teleop_twist_keyboard NVIDIA's original course installs Humble on Ubuntu 22.04. This adaptation's reference setup is Ubuntu 24.04 , which pairs with Jazzy . If you are on Ubuntu 22.04, install Humble instead. # 1. Locale + repo (official instructions: https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Installation/Ubuntu-Install-Debs.html) sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y software-properties-common curl sudo add-apt-repository universe export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION = $( curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F \" '{print $4}' ) curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/ ${ ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION } /ros2-apt-source_ ${ ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION } . $( . /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME ) _all.deb" sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb # 2. ROS 2 Jazzy desktop (includes rviz2) + what the course uses sudo apt update sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-desktop ros-jazzy-teleop-twist-keyboard ros-jazzy-vision-msgs Use it in every new terminal that talks to Isaac Sim: source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION = rmw_fastrtps_cpp # same RMW as Isaac Sim's default ros2 topic list # with Isaac Sim playing a ROS graph you should see its topics Rules of thumb # Keep ROS_DOMAIN_ID the same (or unset) in Isaac Sim's terminal and your ROS terminals. ROS topics only exist while the simulation is playing . Press Play first. To use your system Jazzy inside Isaac Sim (e.g. custom message packages), source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash before running ./isaac-sim.sh . Never try to fix LD_LIBRARY_PATH in an already running Isaac Sim; close it and relaunch from a correctly sourced terminal.

pages.title: Module 1 project
pages.text: Module 1 — Building Your First Robot (project) # Project goal: a four-wheeled robot you built from primitives, driven with the keyboard, whose 2D lidar streams to ROS 2 and shows up in RViz. # Lesson Video Diagram(s) Checkpoint 1.1 Building a simple robot ▶ 1.1 ladder · structure m1_build_simple_robot.py 1.2 Controlling the robot ▶ 1.2 controller graph (graph built by the menu tool) 1.3 Adding sensors ▶ 1.3 sensor mounting m1_ros2_lidar.py 1.4 ROS 2 + RViz ▶ 1.4 data path m1_ros2_lidar.py Project milestones # [ ] The robot drives straight on fixed drives (1.1) — m1_build_simple_robot.py --headless --test passes [ ] W A S D drives and turns it (1.2) [ ] Robot_Camera view follows the robot; RTX lidar sits on the chassis above the wheels (1.3) [ ] ros2 topic hz /scan_lidar ≈ 10 Hz and RViz shows the obstacles (1.4) — m1_ros2_lidar.py --headless --test passes Stretch project: add a 3D lidar (Ouster OS1) and a second camera looking backwards, publish both, and build an RViz config that shows the robot's surroundings while you drive. Take it beyond the checklist # Drive toward an obstacle, then turn so the lidar sees a different part of the scene. Explain how the camera image and the scan represent the same surroundings differently. Save your scene and one observation you can reproduce. Next, import Carter in Module 2 . You will reuse what you learned about bodies, joints, and drives while letting an importer construct the robot.

pages.title: 1.1 Building a simple robot
pages.text: Lesson 1.1: Building a Simple Robot (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Your first robot starts as five separate shapes. By the end of this lesson, its wheels will stay attached, support the chassis, and drive it across the floor. Along the way, you will deliberately make a cube fall and a robot fall apart so you can see what each physics component contributes. Your finish line: save a four-wheeled robot that drives forward when you press Play. Before you begin: launch Isaac Sim and start a new scene. No ROS 2 setup or Python coding is needed for the GUI exercise. Allow 45–60 minutes, plus first-launch loading time. Expected result: with the rear drives at 50 °/s the robot moves about 0.96 m in 3 simulated seconds (50 °/s × 0.375 m ≈ 0.33 m/s). The checkpoint script measures exactly this. Your destination: a frame rendered from the checkpoint scene in Isaac Sim 6.1. Camera, lighting, and display colours were adjusted for readability; geometry and physics were unchanged. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 45–60 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Navigate the viewport and read the Stage / Property panels Tell visual meshes from physics (rigid bodies, colliders, physics scene) Connect bodies with revolute joints and drive them with angular drives Group bodies into an articulation that controllers can address The six-step ladder from mesh to driving robot — interactive HTML You only need three ideas to begin: the Stage panel lists the objects, the Property panel changes the selected object, and Play starts the simulation. The rest will make sense as you build. Part 1: Launch and navigate # cd ~/isaacsim # your Isaac Sim installation folder (contains isaac-sim.sh and python.sh) ./isaac-sim.sh 🔄 6.1: there is no isaac-sim.selector.sh and no Start button. The ROS 2 bridge loads by itself with bundled Jazzy libraries, so leave it on (the course says to disable it in 4.5). The first launch takes a few minutes while shaders compile. Later launches are faster. Viewport navigation hasn't changed: Action Input Fly hold RMB + W A S D , Q / E down/up Look around hold RMB and drag Zoom mouse wheel, or Alt + RMB Pan hold MMB and drag Frame selection F The default stage has World and defaultLight in the Stage panel (top right). The Property panel (bottom right) shows whatever you select. Part 2: Make a cube fall, then catch it # Predict first: if you draw a cube and press Play, will it fall? Try it before adding physics. Keep the simulation stopped while editing; after each experiment, press Stop to reset the scene. Create > Mesh > Cube . Press Play (▶ on the left toolbar, or Space ). The cube stays still. Press Stop . Create > Physics > Physics Scene . The default is Earth gravity along −Z (see the axis gizmo, bottom left). Press Play . Still nothing. Stop before adding the rigid body. Right-click Cube in the Stage panel → Add > Physics > Rigid Body with Colliders Preset . Viewport toolbar eye icon (Show by type) > Physics > Colliders > Selected . A green collision outline appears. Play . The cube falls because it now has a rigid body, but there is no floor to catch it. Stop . Create > Physics > Ground Plane . Expand GroundPlane to see CollisionMesh and CollisionPlane . Select the cube and set Property > Transform > Translate Z = 1 . Play . The cube lands on the ground. Stop (■) resets it. (Optional) Select PhysicsScene and change Gravity Direction , then play. File > Save As… → e.g. learning_resource/output/my_simple_robot.usd . What changed? A visible mesh gives the cube its appearance. A rigid body gives it simulated motion; a collider gives it a shape that can hit the ground. The physics scene supplies gravity and simulation settings. Adding one does not replace the others. Check before continuing: the cube falls onto the ground and Stop returns it to its starting pose. Part 3: Turn the cube into a chassis # The Stage is a tree of prims , the objects and containers in a USD scene. An Xform is a container with a position, rotation, and scale. Group the robot's parts beneath one so you can place them together. Select the cube and set Translate (0, 0, 0) , Scale (2, 1, 0.5) . Right-click empty space in the Stage panel → Create > Xform . Double-click it and rename it to SimpleRobot . Drag Cube onto SimpleRobot , so the cube becomes its child. Select SimpleRobot and set Translate Z = 1 . The cube moves with it (the Xform is a container). Set SimpleRobot Translate Z back to 0 for now. You lift the whole robot in Part 5. Part 4: Add wheels and discover what is missing # Use this map to distinguish front/rear and left/right while naming the parts. Right-click SimpleRobot → Create > Mesh > Cylinder . Set the cylinder's transform: Rotate Scale Translate X 90 0.75, 0.75, 0.25 0.5, 0.75, 0 Rename it Front_Left_Wheel . Duplicate it three times ( Ctrl+D ) and rename and position the copies: Name Translate Front_Left_Wheel 0.5, 0.75 , 0 Front_Right_Wheel 0.5, −0.75 , 0 Rear_Left_Wheel −0.5 , 0.75, 0 Rear_Right_Wheel −0.5 , −0.75, 0 Wheel diameter = 0.75 m, so the radius is 0.375 m . That is larger than half the 0.5 m chassis height: the wheels should touch the ground while the chassis stays above it. Make sure all four wheels and the Cube are children of SimpleRobot. Select the 4 wheels → right-click → Add > Physics > Rigid Body with Colliders Preset . Do the same for Cube if you started a fresh stage. Before pressing Play , predict whether the wheels will stay attached. Try it: the pieces are separate rigid bodies, with no joints to connect them. Stop , then File > Save . You have a robot-shaped collection of objects. Next you will give the connections a physical meaning. Compare your layout with this capture from the completed checkpoint. The robot's +X/front points up; left wheels are on the left. At this stage your own wheels still need joints. Part 5: Keep the wheels attached while letting them turn # A revolute joint connects two bodies while allowing rotation around one axis. For a wheel, that axis must follow its axle. Here it is Y. The wheel was rotated 90° about X, so its local joint frame needs a −90° correction to align with the chassis frame. For each wheel: Click Cube , then Ctrl+click the wheel (body 0 = Cube, body 1 = wheel; order matters). Right-click → Create > Physics > Joint > Revolute Joint . On the new joint, set: Axis = Y Local Rotation 0 = 0, 0, 0 Local Rotation 1 = −90, 0, 0 Deselect and reselect the joint. The red (X) arrows of both frames line up and the blue (Z) arrows match. Arrow direction doesn't matter. Rename it Front_Left_Joint , Front_Right_Joint , Rear_Left_Joint , Rear_Right_Joint . In 6.1 the joint is created under the wheel . You can drag it under SimpleRobot to keep the tree tidy. Finally, select SimpleRobot and set Translate Z = 0.375 , so the wheels rest on the ground plane. Check before continuing: press Play. The wheels should stay attached, and the chassis should rest above the floor. It does not drive yet. Stop before adding the motors. Part 6: Give the rear wheels a motor # A joint allows motion; a drive asks for motion. With stiffness set to zero, the drive responds to a velocity target. Damping controls that response. The target below is in degrees per second . Predict first: both rear wheels will receive +50 °/s. Will the robot move forward or spin? Right-click Rear_Left_Joint → Add > Physics > Angular Drive . Set Damping = 10000 , Stiffness = 0 , Target Velocity = 50 (degrees per second). Repeat for Rear_Right_Joint . Play . The robot drives forward along +X. File > Save . Explain the result: both wheels turn in the same direction, so the robot travels forward. With wheel radius 0.375 m, the ideal rolling speed is (50 × π / 180) × 0.375 ≈ 0.33 m/s . This estimate assumes rolling without slip; it is a useful comparison, not an exact promise. Try one change: set one rear drive to −50 °/s and leave the other at +50 °/s. Predict the motion, then press Play. Stop and restore both to +50 before saving. Why does the robot turn? The driven wheels now try to roll in opposite directions. This produces a turning motion rather than both sides moving forward together. Contact friction and the passive front wheels affect the actual turn. After 3 simulated seconds the chassis has moved about 0.96 m along +X. Compare with its starting position above: the camera did not move. This was driven by the rear joint motors. Troubleshooting # Symptom Fix Robot drags or bounces Wheels must reach lower than the body (check wheel scale 0.75 and Z = 0) Wheels fly off or wobble Joint Body 0 / Body 1 swapped (should be Cube → wheel), or Local Rotation 1 isn't −90, 0, 0 Robot spins instead of moving forward One drive has the opposite sign Something odd Disable joints one at a time ( Joint Enabled checkbox) to find the bad one Compare with the checkpoint # ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m1_build_simple_robot.py # watch it drive ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m1_build_simple_robot.py --headless --test --save learning_resource/output/simple_robot.usd Save your own scene first. Then File > Open learning_resource/output/simple_robot.usd and compare its joints with yours. The checkpoint also adds an Articulation Root , which groups the connected bodies and joints for the controller used in lesson 1.2. Your manual scene adds it in that next lesson. Check your result # Do this You should see Cube alone, Play nothing happens (no physics yet) Cube with rigid body, no ground falls forever Robot with joints, no drives rests on its wheels Rear drives at 50 °/s drives along +X at ≈ 0.33 m/s m1_build_simple_robot.py --headless --test [m1] PASS: robot drove forward Exercises # Set the rear drives to +50 / −50 °/s . What happens, and why? Change the wheel scale to 1.0 (Ø 1 m). Predict the new speed, then measure it (select Cube → Property → Rigid Body → Linear Velocity while playing). Add drives to the front joints too (4-wheel drive). Does it go faster? Why not? Swap Body 0 and Body 1 on one joint and watch what breaks — then undo it. Quiz # Why does a cube with only a Rigid Body (no collider) fall through the ground? Answer Collisions need a collision shape on both prims; the rigid body only adds dynamics. Stiffness 0, damping 10000, target velocity 50 — position or velocity drive? Answer Velocity drive: with zero stiffness only the velocity error produces torque. In what unit is the angular drive's Target Velocity? Answer Degrees per second. Your next mission # You can make the robot move, but its speed is fixed in the joint properties. In lesson 1.2 , connect a controller and use the keyboard to choose when to drive and turn. Save your scene before moving on. Following the original NVIDIA course? This lesson corresponds to “Building Your First Robot → Building a Simple Robot.” See the original learning path and the 6.1 differences when the video menus differ from your screen.

pages.title: 1.2 Controlling the robot
pages.text: Lesson 1.2: Controlling the Robot (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Building Your First Robot → Controlling the Robot ( …/02-controlling-the-robot.html ) Goal: replace the fixed drive velocities with a Differential Controller Action Graph, first driven from the Property panel and then from W A S D . Checkpoint script: scripts/m2_import_carter.py builds this exact graph in code (on Carter, lesson 2.2). The menu tool used below is the same in 4.5 and 6.1. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 30 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Read an Action Graph (OmniGraph): execution vs data connections Use the Differential Controller tool to generate a graph Map keyboard input to robot velocity The Differential Controller Action Graph — interactive HTML Concepts # OmniGraph / Action Graphs. Visual programs stored in the stage. Execution wires (white) say when a node runs; data wires carry values. On Playback Tick fires once per simulated frame, so anything connected to it runs every frame while the timeline plays — and never while stopped. Differential drive kinematics. For wheel radius r and track width d , a body velocity ( v forward, ω turning) becomes wheel speeds ω_left = (v − ω·d/2) / r ω_right = (v + ω·d/2) / r That is all the Differential Controller node computes. Wrong r or d doesn't break the robot — it just makes it drive at the wrong speed or turn by the wrong angle. Articulation Controller. Takes per-joint commands (position, velocity or effort arrays) plus joint names and writes them as drive targets on the articulation. It needs the articulation root to find joints. Part 1: Differential Controller # Open your robot from lesson 1.1 (or learning_resource/output/simple_robot.usd ). Right-click SimpleRobot → Add > Physics > Articulation Root . The controller looks up joints through the articulation, so this has to happen first. (Optional) Set the two rear drives' Target Velocity back to 0 , so only the controller moves the robot. Tools > Robotics > OmniGraph Controllers > Differential Controller 🔄 Same path as 4.5. In 4.2 it was Isaac Utils > Common Omnigraphs . Fill in the dialog (6.1 field names): Field Value graph path leave default /Graphs/differential_controller Robot Prim SimpleRobot (click Add /select in the picker) wheel radius 0.375 (half the 0.75 m wheel) distance between wheels 1.5 Left Joint Name Rear_Left_Joint Right Joint Name Rear_Right_Joint Left/Right Joint Index leave −1 (names are used) Use Keyboard Control (WASD) off for Part 1 Click OK . The Stage panel now has Graphs > differential_controller . Right-click it → Open Graph to see the nodes: On Playback Tick : fires every frame Differential Controller : (linear, angular) velocity → left/right wheel speeds Articulation Controller : applies the wheel speeds to the joints ArrayNames (a Make Array node): the two joint names as tokens. Add inputs to drive more joints 7. Play . Nothing moves, because Desired Linear Velocity = 0. 8. Select the Differential Controller node and set Linear Velocity = 1 (forward), −1 (back), or Angular Velocity = 1 (turn). Keep values small. The robot may hop a bit, because there are no friction materials yet (same as in the course). Part 2: Keyboard control # Before rebuilding the graph, try a short prediction experiment. Keep the physical robot unchanged, set linear velocity to zero, and command angular velocity 1 rad/s. Then double only the controller's wheel-distance value from 1.5 to 3.0. Will it ask the wheels to turn faster or slower? Hint and explanation In the formula above, the turning term is proportional to the configured wheel distance. Doubling that value doubles the requested wheel speeds for a pure turn. The physical track has not changed, so ideal rolling predicts a faster turn; friction and slip affect the measured result. Restore 1.5 before continuing. Stop . Delete the graph from Part 1 (right-click differential_controller → Delete). Tools > Robotics > OmniGraph Controllers > Differential Controller again, with the same values as above, but tick Use Keyboard Control (WASD) . Open the new graph. On the left you'll see four Read Keyboard State nodes (W, A, S, D). Each goes through To Double and Add/Multiply , and is then scaled by the two Constant Double nodes ( ScaleLinear , ScaleAngular ) before reaching the controller's linear/angular inputs. Play , click into the viewport, and drive with W A S D . Too fast or too slow? Change ScaleLinear / ScaleAngular (the speed each key gives). File > Save . 🔄 6.1 detail: the keyboard nodes are omni.graph.nodes.ReadKeyboardState . If an old 4.x graph uses deprecated node names, isaacsim.core.deprecation_manager migrates them when you open the file. Troubleshooting # Symptom Fix "Robot Prim" can't be picked / controller does nothing Add Articulation Root to SimpleRobot first Robot turns when it should go straight Left/right joint names swapped Keys do nothing Click inside the viewport so it has keyboard focus, and make sure the simulation is playing Robot wanders back and forth Old fixed drive velocities (50) are still set. Set them to 0 Check your result # Do this You should see Play with Linear Velocity 0 robot stands still Linear Velocity 1 drives forward ≈ 1 m/s Angular Velocity 1 turns left (counter-clockwise from above) Keyboard graph, hold W drives forward; A/D turn Exercises # Keep the wheel-distance setting correct and halve only the configured wheel radius. Predict the change in requested wheel speed for straight driving, test briefly, then restore 0.375 m. Make Shift+W a faster forward key (the keyboard nodes accept a modifier). Add the front joints to ArrayNames (4 names) and feed the controller output twice — what has to change in the graph? Quiz # Why does nothing happen in the graph while the simulation is stopped? Answer Everything hangs off On Playback Tick, which only fires while the timeline plays. What does the Articulation Controller need in order to find the joints? Answer An articulation root on the robot (and the joint names). v = 1 m/s, ω = 0, r = 0.375 m — wheel speed? Answer 1 / 0.375 ≈ 2.67 rad/s on both wheels.

pages.title: 1.3 Adding sensors
pages.text: Lesson 1.3: Adding Sensors (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Building Your First Robot → Adding Sensors ( …/03-adding-sensors.html ) Goal: mount an RGB camera and a 2D lidar on the robot and look at what they see. Checkpoint script: scripts/m1_ros2_lidar.py (also covers lesson 1.4) Expected result: an RTX 2D lidar on the chassis publishes /scan_lidar at ~10 Hz, and its forward beam reads 2.50 m to an obstacle placed 2.50 m ahead. 🔄 Biggest change in this module. The course uses a PhysX Lidar ( Create > Sensors > PhysX Lidar > Rotating ). In 6.1 that extension is deprecated ( extsDeprecated/isaacsim.sensors.physx ). It still appears in the menu, but this lesson uses its replacement, an RTX Lidar with the 2D config Example Rotary 2D . If you want to follow the video exactly, the PhysX steps are in the collapsible section at the end. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 45 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Mount a camera on a fixed-jointed sensor body Add an RTX lidar (the 6.1 replacement of the PhysX lidar) in a place where it works Understand how RTX sensors see the scene (rendering, not physics) Where each sensor goes in Isaac Sim 6.1 — interactive HTML Concepts # Two kinds of lidar. The course's PhysX lidar casts physics rays — it only hits colliders . Isaac Sim 6.1's RTX lidar is simulated by the RTX renderer — it hits everything rendered , models real sensor scan patterns (vendor configs like Ouster, Hesai, SICK) and outputs a GenericModelOutput buffer that helper nodes turn into LaserScan / PointCloud2 . Sensors ride on bodies. A sensor prim follows whatever body it is parented to. Under a rigid body it moves with that body; under a plain Xform beside the bodies it stays behind when the robot drives off. The 6.1 trap. An RTX lidar under a separate rigid body that is fixed-jointed to the chassis produced no output in our tests (topic exists, zero messages). Under the chassis body itself it works. Nova Carter mounts all its sensors that way ( chassis_link/sensors/... ), so do the same. Units under a scaled parent. Cube is scaled (2, 1, 0.5). A child's Translate is multiplied by that scale: (0.45, 0, 1.0) → 0.9 m forward, 0.5 m up. The ranges the lidar reports are still in metres (verified: an obstacle 2.50 m ahead reads 2.50 m). Part 1: Sensor mount (Front_Sensor) # Right-click SimpleRobot → Create > Xform . Rename it Front_Sensor . Move it to the top front of the body: Translate (0.9, 0, 0.35) (relative to SimpleRobot). Right-click Front_Sensor → Add > Physics > Rigid Body . Known issue (also in the course): if Rigid Body can't be added, temporarily move Front_Sensor's children out, add it, then move them back. Fixed joint to the chassis: click Cube , Ctrl+click Front_Sensor → right-click → Create > Physics > Joint > Fixed Joint . Check Body 0 = Cube and Body 1 = Front_Sensor . If they're swapped, fix them with the folder icon. Right-click Front_Sensor → Create > Mesh > Cube , set Scale (0.1, 0.1, 0.1) , and rename it Sensor_Mount . (The course also adds Rigid Body with Colliders Preset to Sensor_Mount. A collider is enough. A second rigid body nested inside Front_Sensor isn't needed.) Part 2: RGB camera # Right-click Sensor_Mount → Create > Camera . Rename it Robot_Camera . Point it forward: Rotate Y = −90 (the course value). If the image is upside down or sideways, set Rotate to (90, −90, 0) instead (the value lesson 2.3 uses for Carter). Move it to the front edge of the mount. Look through it: at the top of the viewport, open the camera menu (shows Perspective ) → Cameras > Robot_Camera . Switch back to Perspective when you're done. Tip: while you look through Robot_Camera, RMB+WASD moves the camera prim . Switch back before navigating. Add some obstacles: Create > Mesh > Cube / Cone / Cylinder , spread out in front of the robot. Two views at once: 🔄 Window > Viewports > Viewport 2 (4.2: Window > Viewport > Viewport 2 ). Set Viewport 1 to Perspective and Viewport 2 to Robot_Camera . Play and drive with W A S D. The camera view follows the robot. Part 3: 2D lidar (RTX) # ⚠️ 6.1 trap, found while testing this lesson. The course puts the lidar on Front_Sensor , a separate rigid body held by a Fixed Joint. In 6.1 an RTX lidar mounted on a fixed-jointed body publishes nothing (no errors, just no data). It works when the lidar sits directly on the chassis body , which is also how NVIDIA's Nova Carter mounts its sensors. The camera from Part 2 is fine on Front_Sensor. Select Cube (the chassis rigid body). 🔄 Create > Sensors > RTX Lidar > NVIDIA > Example Rotary 2D (4.5 course: Create > Sensors > PhysX Lidar > Rotating ). It's created as a child of Cube, named Example_Rotary_2D . Set its Translate = (0.45, 0, 1.0) . These are Cube-local units. Cube is scaled (2, 1, 0.5), so this means 0.9 m forward and 0.5 m above the chassis centre (≈ 0.875 m above the ground). Why this high? The wheel tops are at 0.75 m. A lidar below that sees the robot's own wheels (tested: at 0.725 m the closest "obstacle" was the rear wheel). Seeing the beams. RTX lidars don't have the PhysX Draw Lines / Draw Points checkboxes. Ways to see the data: * lesson 1.4 : publish to ROS 2 and view it in RViz (what the course does next anyway), or * from Python: attach the draw-point-cloud writer: python # Window > Script Editor, with the simulation stopped from isaacsim.sensors.experimental.rtx import Lidar, LidarSensor lidar = Lidar("/World/SimpleRobot/Cube/Example_Rotary_2D") sensor = LidarSensor(lidar, annotators=[]) sensor.attach_writer("draw-point-cloud", size=0.05, color=[1.0, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0]) Then press Play . Red points appear where the beams hit. Obstacle detection: an RTX lidar sees every rendered surface , so the obstacles show up even without colliders. That's different from the PhysX lidar in the course. Still give them Add > Physics > Rigid Body with Colliders Preset , so the robot can't drive through them. File > Save. Placing prims by script? Prims made with Create > Mesh have translate / orient / scale ops. UsdGeom.XformCommonAPI(prim).SetTranslate(...) silently does nothing on them. Set prim.GetAttribute("xformOp:translate").Set(...) instead. (This bit us while writing the checkpoint script.) Course-exact alternative: PhysX Lidar (deprecated in 6.1) Select Front_Sensor → Create > Sensors > PhysX Lidar > Rotating (the PhysX lidar is fine on Front_Sensor; the trap above is RTX-only). Stop the simulation, select the lidar, open Raw USD Properties , and tick drawLines and drawPoints . Play . Gray beams mean no hit, red beams mean a hit. PhysX lidar beams only hit colliders , so the obstacles need Rigid Body with Colliders Preset . Slow the rotation ( rotationRate ) to inspect the beams. Raise the lidar if it hits the wheels. Expect a deprecation warning in the console. The ROS 2 graph for this sensor ( Isaac Read Lidar Beams , isaacsim.sensors.physx.IsaacReadLidarBeams ) is also deprecated. Check your result # Do this You should see Viewport → Cameras → Robot_Camera you see the scene from the robot's front Drive with W while in Viewport 2 = Robot_Camera camera view moves with the robot Lidar prim type in Property panel OmniLidar , under /World/SimpleRobot/Cube m1_ros2_lidar.py --headless --test forward beam = 2.50 m … PASS Exercises # Lower the lidar to Translate z = 0.7 and look at the scan in RViz (lesson 1.4). Where do the extra close points come from? Swap Example Rotary 2D for Create > Sensors > RTX Lidar > Ouster > OS1 and publish Point Cloud instead of Laser Scan . Put a cone behind a glass-like thin plane without a collider. Which lidar type would see the plane — PhysX or RTX? Quiz # Does an RTX lidar need colliders on obstacles to detect them? Answer No — it renders the scene; colliders only matter for physical contact. Where must the RTX lidar be mounted on SimpleRobot in 6.1? Answer Directly under the chassis rigid body (Cube), not on the fixed-jointed Front_Sensor. Why place the lidar above 0.75 m? Answer Below the wheel tops the scan hits the robot's own wheels.

pages.title: 1.4 ROS 2 and RViz
pages.text: Lesson 1.4: Accessing Data — Lidar to ROS 2 and RViz (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Building Your First Robot → Accessing Data ( …/04-accessing-data.html ) Goal: publish the robot's 2D lidar as a ROS 2 sensor_msgs/LaserScan on /scan_lidar and view it in RViz. Checkpoint script: scripts/m1_ros2_lidar.py Expected result: about 10 LaserScan messages per second on /scan_lidar (frame sim_lidar , 3600 beams). Prerequisite: system ROS 2 Jazzy for ros2 and rviz2 , see ../01_setup_ros2_jazzy.md 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 45 min (+ ROS 2 install) · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Publish simulated sensor data on ROS 2 topics Inspect topics with the ros2 CLI and visualise them in RViz2 Understand frames, QoS and domain IDs — the three usual reasons for 'no data' RTX lidar → ROS 2 LaserScan → RViz — interactive HTML Concepts # ROS 2 in one paragraph. Programs ( nodes ) exchange typed messages on named topics through DDS. Nodes find each other automatically when they share a ROS_DOMAIN_ID and a compatible middleware (RMW). Isaac Sim's bridge is just another node living inside the simulator. Frames. Every sensor message carries header.frame_id . RViz draws data relative to its Fixed Frame ; if no transform connects the two, nothing is drawn. With only one frame ( sim_lidar ), set the Fixed Frame to exactly that name. QoS. Sensor streams are published best-effort (drop old data rather than queue it). rviz2 and ros2 topic echo adapt automatically; your own subscriber must use qos_profile_sensor_data . Bundled vs system ROS. Isaac Sim loads its own Jazzy libraries ( exts/isaacsim.ros2.core/jazzy ). System ROS is only needed for tools you run outside — and must be sourced in those terminals. Part 1: ROS 2 (what changed) # Course (4.5, Ubuntu 22.04) 6.1 reference setup (Ubuntu 24.04) Install ROS 2 Humble Install ROS 2 Jazzy (only for rviz2 / ros2 CLI) source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash before ./isaac-sim.sh Not needed. Isaac Sim loads its bundled Jazzy libs. Just run ./isaac-sim.sh Enable the ROS2 Bridge in Window > Extensions Already enabled at startup ( isaacsim.ros2.bridge ). Check it under Window > Extensions if unsure Install vision_msgs Bundled. Install ros-jazzy-vision-msgs on the system side only if a ROS tool needs it Part 2: Open your project # ./isaac-sim.sh → File > Open Recent → your robot from lesson 1.3. (Optional) Window > Viewports > Viewport 2 for a robot-camera view. Part 3: Build the lidar → ROS 2 graph # 🔄 The course builds this by hand ( Isaac Read Lidar Beams → ROS2 Publish Laser Scan + Isaac Read Simulation Time ), and those nodes only work with the PhysX lidar. For the RTX lidar from lesson 1.3, 6.1 has a one-click graph builder. Stop the simulation, then: Tools > Robotics > ROS 2 OmniGraphs > RTX Lidar Fill in the dialog: Field Value Graph Path /World/ROS2_LidarStream (the course's graph name) Frame ID sim_lidar (remember this for RViz) Node Namespace empty LaserScan Topic scan_lidar Lidar Prim pick your RTX lidar, /World/SimpleRobot/Cube/Example_Rotary_2D Laser Scan ✅ ticked Point Cloud optional (publishes /point_cloud as PointCloud2) OK . Open the graph to see what it made: On Playback Tick → Isaac Run One Simulation Frame → Isaac Create Render Product (the lidar) → ROS2 RTX Lidar Helper (type laser_scan ), plus a ROS2 Context . The helper does the work of the course's Read Lidar Beams + Publish Laser Scan + Read Simulation Time chain. The Laser Scan output only works with a 2D lidar config ( Example Rotary 2D ). For a 3D lidar, publish Point Cloud instead. Course-exact manual graph (PhysX lidar only) Create > Visual Scripting > Action Graph , rename it ROS2_LidarStream , and add: On Playback Tick , Isaac Read Lidar Beams Node , ROS2 Publish Laser Scan , Isaac Read Simulation Time . Connect Tick → Read Lidar Beams (exec), Read Lidar Beams outputs → matching Publish Laser Scan inputs (exec, azimuthRange, depthRange, horizontalFov, horizontalResolution, intensitiesData, linearDepthData, numCols, numRows, rotationRate), and Read Simulation Time → Publish Laser Scan timeStamp . Set the lidar prim on Read Lidar Beams, topicName = scan_lidar , frameId = sim_lidar . Part 4: Run and view in RViz # Play in Isaac Sim. New terminal: bash source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash ros2 topic list # expect /scan_lidar, /rosout, /parameter_events ros2 topic hz /scan_lidar # ~10 Hz rviz2 In RViz: Global Options > Fixed Frame = sim_lidar , typed in. (The course text says to use the topic name. That's wrong: Fixed Frame must be the Frame ID .) Add (bottom left) → By topic → /scan_lidar → LaserScan → OK. Red points show the obstacles. Raise Size (m) to 0.05 if they're hard to see. Drive with W A S D in Isaac Sim. In RViz the world moves around the fixed robot, because the scan is drawn in the lidar's own frame. File > Save . Checkpoint # # needs learning_resource/output/simple_robot.usd (from m1_build_simple_robot.py --save ...) ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m1_ros2_lidar.py # leaves the sim running for RViz ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m1_ros2_lidar.py --headless --test # subscribes to /scan_lidar itself Troubleshooting # Symptom Fix No /scan_lidar in ros2 topic list Simulation not playing , or different ROS_DOMAIN_ID in the two terminals Topic listed but ros2 topic echo prints nothing RMW mismatch. export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_fastrtps_cpp in the ROS terminal RViz: "Frame [sim_lidar] does not exist" / nothing drawn Fixed Frame must be typed exactly sim_lidar Scan shows a ring of points around the robot Lidar is too low and sees the wheels/body. Raise it "is not a valid RTX lidar prim" when creating the graph You picked the Xform/mount, not the lidar prim (type OmniLidar ) /scan_lidar is listed but no messages ever arrive The RTX lidar is on a fixed-jointed sensor body (lesson 1.3 trap). Move it directly under the chassis body Messages arrive in ros2 topic echo but a custom subscriber gets none QoS: the scan is published best-effort. Subscribe with qos_profile_sensor_data Check your result # Do this You should see ros2 topic list while playing /scan_lidar is listed ros2 topic hz /scan_lidar ≈ 10 Hz ros2 topic echo /scan_lidar --once frame_id: sim_lidar , 3600 ranges RViz, Fixed Frame sim_lidar , LaserScan display points on your obstacles Exercises # Tick Point Cloud in the RTX Lidar graph dialog too and add a PointCloud2 display in RViz. Run export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7 in the RViz terminal only. What happens? Fix it. Write a 15-line rclpy node that prints the closest range in front of the robot (remember qos_profile_sensor_data ). Quiz # RViz says 'Frame [sim_lidar] does not exist'. What do you change? Answer Set Global Options → Fixed Frame to `sim_lidar` (the frame id, not the topic). Do you need to source /opt/ros/jazzy before ./isaac-sim.sh? Answer No — 6.1 uses its bundled Jazzy libraries. ros2 topic echo shows data but your node gets nothing. Likely cause? Answer QoS mismatch: subscribe with the sensor-data (best-effort) profile.

pages.title: 2.1 Importing URDF
pages.text: Lesson 2.1: Importing URDF Assets (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Ingesting Robot Assets and Simulating Your Robot → Importing URDF Assets ( …/ingesting-robot-assets-and-simulating-your-robot-in-isaac-sim/01-importing-urdf-assets.html ) Goal: import Carter (two drive wheels plus a passive caster) from carter.urdf and get a USD robot with correct drives. Checkpoint script: scripts/m2_import_carter.py (lessons 2.1 + 2.2) Expected result: the imported Carter drives about 0.6 m in 3 s at 0.2 m/s with a Differential Controller. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 30 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Import a URDF with the rewritten 6.1 importer Understand the generated asset: payloads, Physics variant set , Geometry vs Physics scopes Configure joint drives by hand (the 6.1 dialog no longer does it) URDF → drivable USD robot in 6.1 — interactive HTML What the 6.1 importer writes — interactive HTML Concepts # URDF vs USD. URDF (ROS) describes links (rigid parts with visuals/collisions/inertia) and joints (how links move relative to each other). USD describes a scene . The importer maps links → rigid body Xforms under Geometry , joints → PhysicsRevoluteJoint /… under Physics . Layered assets. The 6.1 converter writes carter.usda (the entry file) plus payloads/ ( base , geometries , materials , Physics/physx|mujoco|physics ). Layers let one asset carry several physics descriptions; a variant set called Physics chooses which one is loaded. No selection = no physics layer = a robot that neither falls nor moves. Drives after import. URDF has no notion of "this joint is motorised with gain X", so the importer creates angular drives with zero gains. You decide: wheels → velocity drives (stiffness 0, damping > 0), casters → passive (both 0). Get the URDF # You don't need the course's carter.zip . The same Carter URDF ships with Isaac Sim 6.1. Copy it into the course folder once, so the importer writes its output next to your course files instead of inside Isaac Sim's own extension folder: cd ~/isaacsim # your Isaac Sim installation folder mkdir -p learning_resource/assets cp -r exts/isaacsim.asset.importer.urdf/data/urdf/robots/carter learning_resource/assets/ You now have learning_resource/assets/carter/urdf/carter.urdf and …/carter/meshes/*.obj . (The checkpoint script does this copy automatically if the folder is missing. The files are part of Isaac Sim and are not redistributed with this course.) Import (6.1 workflow) # 🔄 The 6.1 importer is a rewrite ( isaacsim.asset.importer.urdf 3.x, based on the open-source urdf-usd-converter ). The menu is still File > Import , but the options changed: 4.5 6.1 Links → Moveable base Options → Base Type → Mobile Joints and Drives → Natural Frequency + per-joint Target Type gone from the dialog : set drives after import (Part 3) One .usd file, imported into your stage A folder carter/carter.usda + payloads/ , opened as a new stage unless Add Reference to Stage is ticked ./isaac-sim.sh , then File > New . File > Import → browse to learning_resource/assets/carter/urdf/ → select carter.urdf . The options panel on the right: Section Option Value Model USD Output leave Same as Imported Model (Default) → writes assets/carter/urdf/carter/carter.usda . Or pick learning_resource/output/ Model ROS Package List leave empty (the meshes use package://carter/... , found by scanning the folders) Colliders Collision From Visuals off (the URDF has its own collision shapes) Colliders Allow Self-Collision off Options Robot Type Default (or Wheeled Robot , if listed) Options Base Type Mobile Options Add Reference to Stage off for now (the robot opens on its own, so you can inspect it) Options Merge Mesh / Debug Mode off Click Import . After a few seconds the converted carter.usda opens as the current stage. What you get: the 6.1 asset structure # Expand carter in the Stage panel: carter (default prim, has a "Physics" variant set) ├── Geometry │ └── chassis_link (rigid body + ArticulationRoot) │ ├── left_wheel_link │ ├── right_wheel_link │ ├── rear_pivot_link │ │ └── rear_wheel_link │ ├── com_offset, imu ├── Physics (joints live here, not under the links) │ ├── left_wheel right_wheel rear_pivot rear_axle (revolute) │ └── root_joint … ├── Materials / VisualMaterials ⚠️ Select the physics variant # Select carter → Property panel → Variants → Physics = physx . The importer writes one physics layer per engine ( physx , mujoco , physics = plain USD Physics, none ). Until you pick one, the joints and rigid bodies aren't loaded, and the robot won't move. Part 3: Set the drives (replaces "Joints and Drives" from 4.5) # The importer gives every revolute joint an Angular Drive with stiffness 0 and damping 0 , so nothing is driven yet. Set them by hand to match the course (wheels = Velocity, caster joints = None): Joint ( /carter/Physics/… ) Course target type 6.1 setting in Property > Drive > Angular left_wheel Velocity Stiffness 0 , Damping 10000 right_wheel Velocity Stiffness 0 , Damping 10000 rear_pivot None Stiffness 0, Damping 0 (passive) rear_axle None Stiffness 0, Damping 0 (passive) Velocity drive = stiffness 0, damping > 0: the joint tracks Target Velocity . Position drive = stiffness > 0. None = both 0. File > Save (this saves into the carter.usda layer you have open). Scripted alternative: URDFImporterConfig accepts joint_target_type , override_joint_stiffness and override_joint_damping (per joint via a dict). The GUI just doesn't expose them. Checkpoint # ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m2_import_carter.py # import + scene + drive, with a window ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m2_import_carter.py --headless --test # self-check The script writes learning_resource/output/carter/carter.usda . You can reference that file in later lessons. Check your result # Do this You should see Stage panel after import carter > Geometry , Physics , Materials carter → Property → Variants Physics = physx left_wheel → Drive stiffness 0, damping 10000 m2_import_carter.py --headless --test [m2] PASS: Carter drove forward Exercises # Open learning_resource/output/carter/payloads/Physics/physics.usda in a text editor and find the left_wheel joint. Which body is body0? Switch the variant to mujoco and press Play. What happens with the PhysX engine running? Re-import with Base Type = Fixed . What changed in Physics/ ? Quiz # The imported Carter doesn't fall when you press Play. First thing to check? Answer The Physics variant — select physx. Where are the joints in the 6.1 asset? Answer Under `/carter/Physics/`. Which gains make a joint a velocity drive? Answer Stiffness 0 and damping > 0.

pages.title: 2.2 Preparing the simulation
pages.text: Lesson 2.2: Preparing the Simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Ingesting Robot Assets → Preparing the Simulation ( …/02-preparing-the-simulation.html ) Goal: put Carter in an environment, check its joints, and drive it with W A S D through a Differential Controller. Checkpoint script: scripts/m2_import_carter.py 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 30 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Compose a scene from referenced assets Read controller parameters straight out of the URDF Limit speeds so a controller behaves Where the Differential Controller numbers come from — interactive HTML Concepts # References. Dragging carter.usda into a stage creates a reference : the robot's data stays in its file, your scene stores only "load that file here" plus your overrides (position, variant choice, drive gains you change later). That's why the variant must be selected again per reference. Parameters from the source. The controller needs wheel radius and track width. Don't guess — the URDF says: wheel <cylinder radius="0.240"> and wheel joints at y = ±0.3142 → track 0.6284 m. Saturation. Keyboard graphs command step changes; without maxLinearSpeed / maxAngularSpeed the wheels saturate, slip and the robot hops. Limits are a cheap way to keep a sim stable. Part 1: Environment # 🔄 The importer opened carter.usda as its own stage. Build a scene around it instead: File > New . 🔄 Create > Environments > Flat Grid (4.2: Create > Isaac > Environments > Flat Grid ). Add the robot to this stage, either way works: * drag carter.usda from the Content browser (bottom panel) into the viewport, or * File > Import carter.urdf again with Add Reference to Stage ticked. Select the new carter prim → Variants > Physics = physx (the variant choice is stored per reference, so set it again here). Turn off the scene's environment light by clicking the 👁 next to it in the Stage panel (optional, as in the course). Raise Carter a little: Transform > Translate Z = 0.05 . Play . Carter drops onto the grid. Stop . Hide collision outlines: viewport eye > Physics > Colliders > None . Part 2: Joint review # All joints are under carter > Physics (4.5: a joints folder, 4.2: under chassis_link ): Joint Body 0 Body 1 Axis left_wheel chassis_link left_wheel_link Y right_wheel chassis_link right_wheel_link Y rear_pivot chassis_link rear_pivot_link Z (caster swivel) rear_axle rear_pivot_link rear_wheel_link Y Part 3: Quick drive test (no controller) # Select left_wheel and right_wheel → Drive > Angular > Target Velocity = 20 (°/s). (They need the velocity drive from lesson 2.1: stiffness 0, damping 10000.) Play . Carter rolls forward slowly (20 °/s × 0.24 m ≈ 0.08 m/s). While it's playing, set one wheel back to 0 . Carter turns. Stop and set both targets back to 0 . The course's "Articulation Root fix (4.2 only)" is not needed : the 6.1 importer already puts the articulation root on chassis_link with self-collisions off. Part 4: Differential Controller with keyboard # Tools > Robotics > OmniGraph Controllers > Differential Controller : Field Value Where it comes from Robot Prim carter wheel radius 0.24 wheel collision cylinder radius in the URDF distance between wheels 0.62 (exact: 0.6284) 2 × the 0.3142 m wheel Y offset Left Joint Name left_wheel Right Joint Name right_wheel Use Keyboard Control (WASD) ✅ OK → Stage panel Graphs > differential_controller → right-click → Open Graph . Play , click the viewport, and drive with W A S D . Part 5: Speed limits # The keyboard graph commands large speeds, and Carter becomes erratic. Select the Differential Controller node in the graph and set: Property Value maxLinearSpeed 0.5 m/s (the course used 0.2 in 4.5 and 0.5 in 4.2) maxAngularSpeed 1.0 rad/s Check it: select chassis_link → Property > Rigid Body velocity while holding W . It should stay under the limit. File > Save As… learning_resource/output/carter_scene.usd . Troubleshooting # Symptom Fix Carter doesn't fall / doesn't react Physics variant not set to physx on this reference Wheels spin but Carter doesn't move Wheels intersect the grid: raise Carter, or check the drives have damping Carter spins in place with W One of the joint names is wrong in the controller dialog Caster wheel fights the motion rear_pivot / rear_axle must be passive (stiffness 0, damping 0) Check your result # Do this You should see Play after adding the reference Carter drops onto the grid and rests Both wheel targets 20 °/s ≈ 0.08 m/s straight Keyboard graph, hold W ≤ 0.5 m/s (chassis_link → Rigid Body velocity) Exercises # Set wheel radius to 0.12 (half the real value) and drive forward at 0.2 m/s. Measure the real speed. Why is it double? Make the casters slightly damped (damping 10). Is turning smoother or worse? Save the scene, close Isaac Sim, edit carter.usda 's drive gains in a text editor and reopen — does your scene pick up the change? (That's what references buy you.) Quiz # Why must the physics variant be selected again in a new scene? Answer The selection is an override stored on the referencing prim, not in carter.usda. Where does wheelDistance 0.6284 come from? Answer 2 × the wheel joint y-offset 0.3142 in the URDF. Why limit maxLinearSpeed? Answer Keyboard steps saturate the wheels and make the robot slip and hop.

pages.title: 2.3 Adding sensors
pages.text: Lesson 2.3: Adding Sensors to Carter (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Ingesting Robot Assets → Adding Sensors ( …/03-adding-sensors.html ) Goal: add an RGB camera and a lidar to the imported Carter and see obstacles with both. Start from your Carter scene from lesson 2.2 ( learning_resource/output/carter_scene.usd ). 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 30 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Apply the module-1 sensor rules to an imported robot Edit a referenced asset (and know when your edits land in which file) Sensors on the imported Carter — interactive HTML Concepts # Where do edits go? Adding a prim under a referenced robot writes an override into your scene file, not into carter.usda . Usually that's what you want (the sensor belongs to this experiment). To make the sensor part of the robot asset, open carter.usda itself and add it there. Sensor frames. Camera prims look down their local −Z with +Y up; the course's rotation (90, −90, 0) turns that into "look along the robot's +X". If an image is sideways, it's always this rotation. RGB camera # Move the viewport close to Carter. Create > Camera . In the Stage panel, drag it under carter > Geometry > chassis_link . 🔄 6.1 path: carter/Geometry/chassis_link (4.5: Carter/chassis_link ). If the reference won't accept children, that's because you're editing a referenced asset. Put the camera in the same spot by opening carter.usda itself ( File > Open ) and saving it there. Or keep the camera outside the robot and attach it with a fixed joint, as in lesson 1.3. Rename it RGB_Sensor . Translate (0.1, 0.0, 0.33) , Rotate (90, −90, 0) . Turn off snapping (magnet icon, left toolbar) if the values jump. Viewport camera menu → Cameras > RGB_Sensor to check the view. Switch back to Perspective . Play , drive with W A S D , and confirm the camera moves with Carter. Stop . Lidar # 🔄 Course: Create > Isaac > Sensors > PhysX Lidar > Rotating (4.2 path, PhysX lidar). 6.1: use the RTX lidar. Same reasons as lesson 1.3. Select chassis_link → Create > Sensors > RTX Lidar > NVIDIA > Example Rotary 2D (for a 3D scan, use Example Rotary or a real model, e.g. Ouster , HESAI , SICK ). Make sure it's under chassis_link . Translate (−0.05, 0.0, 0.42) . To see the beams, use the draw-point-cloud writer snippet from lesson 1.3, Part 3 , or publish to ROS 2 and view it in RViz ( lesson 1.4 ). Obstacles # Create > Mesh > Cube / Sphere / Cylinder : place several around the grid at different distances and angles. Play . * PhysX lidar (course): beams stay gray until the obstacles get colliders. * RTX lidar (6.1): obstacles are detected right away , because RTX sees rendered geometry. Stop , select all obstacles → right-click → Add > Physics > Rigid Body with Colliders Preset (so Carter physically bumps into them). Play , switch the viewport to RGB_Sensor , and drive with W A S D . Stop , and switch back to Perspective . Otherwise navigating the viewport moves the camera prim. File > Save. Check your result # Do this You should see Viewport → Cameras → RGB_Sensor view from Carter's front Lidar prim path …/chassis_link/Example_Rotary_2D Drive into an obstacle with colliders Carter is stopped by it Exercises # Publish this lidar to ROS 2 (lesson 1.4 dialog) and view it in RViz while driving. Add a second camera looking backwards. Which rotation do you need? Quiz # You added a camera under the referenced carter. Which file stores it? Answer Your scene file (as an override), not carter.usda. Why does the RTX lidar see obstacles without colliders? Answer It is rendered, not physics-based.

pages.title: 2.4 Nova Carter
pages.text: Lesson 2.4: Accessing a Prepared Robot: Nova Carter (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Ingesting Robot Assets → Accessing a Prepared Robot ( …/04-accessing-a-prepared-robot.html ) Goal: load NVIDIA's ready-made Nova Carter , which already has physics, drives and a full sensor suite, and compare it with the Carter you built by hand. 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 15 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Load a production robot asset Read a real sensor suite and joint layout Nova Carter's ready-made sensor suite — interactive HTML Concepts # Why prepared assets? Nova Carter took NVIDIA engineers tuned masses, drive gains, collision shapes, materials and calibrated sensor models. For real projects you start here and only build robots yourself when no asset exists (then via URDF → USD as in lesson 2.1). Robot-type layout. Notice the pattern you will see in most 6.x robots: one articulation root body, sensors/ as plain Xforms beneath it, joints named joint_* . File > New . 🔄 Create > Environments > Flat Grid (4.2: Create > Isaac > Environments > FlatGrid ). Hide the environment light (👁 in the Stage panel) if you like. 🔄 Create > Robots > Nova Carter with Sensors (same as 4.5). It loads /Isaac/Robots/NVIDIA/NovaCarter/nova_carter.usd from the NVIDIA asset server. The first load can take a few minutes. (Optional) The finished version of the URDF Carter, Carter_v1 : 🔄 Window > Browsers > Isaac Sim Assets → search carter → drag Carter_v1 (or carter_v1 ) into the stage. (4.5: Isaac Sim Assets [Beta] panel.) Review the robot # Expand nova_carter > chassis_link in the Stage panel: Checked in this install (6.1 nova_carter.usd ). Everything below is under chassis_link/sensors/ : Sensor Prim Type 2 × 2D lidar (front / rear) front_RPLidar/RPLidar_S2E , rear_RPLidar/RPLidar_S2E RTX OmniLidar (Slamtec RPLidar S2E) 1 × 3D lidar on top XT_32/PandarXT_32_10hz RTX OmniLidar (Hesai XT-32, 10 Hz) 4 × Hawk stereo cameras front_hawk , left_hawk , right_hawk , back_hawk , each with left / right cameras + an IMU Camera + IsaacImuSensor 4 × Owl fisheye cameras front_owl , left_owl , right_owl , back_owl → camera Camera chassis IMU chassis_imu/Imu_Sensor IsaacImuSensor Drive and joints ( nova_carter/… ): Part Joints 2 driven wheels (radius 0.14 m, track 0.413 m) joint_wheel_left , joint_wheel_right 2 passive casters at the back joint_caster_base , joint_swing_left/right , joint_caster_left/right articulation root chassis_link , the target for the Articulation Controller in lesson 4.1 Notice that every sensor sits under the chassis body ( chassis_link/sensors/... ), not on a separate fixed-jointed body. That's the mounting that works for RTX lidars in 6.1 (see the trap in lesson 1.3). Compare with your URDF Carter: Nova Carter comes with tuned drives, collision shapes, materials and sensors, so there's no manual setup. In 6.1 you may see Projection type 'fisheyePolynomial' is deprecated warnings for the Owl/Hawk cameras in the console. They're harmless. The asset still works. Next: drive Nova Carter from ROS 2 in lesson 4.1 . Check your result # Do this You should see Create > Robots > Nova Carter with Sensors /World/nova_carter appears Expand chassis_link/sensors front/rear RPLidar, XT_32, 4× Hawk, 4× Owl, chassis_imu Exercises # Look through front_hawk/left/camera_left (Viewport camera menu). Find the drive gains of joint_wheel_left . How do they compare with what you set on Carter? Quiz # Which prim is Nova Carter's articulation root? Answer `chassis_link`. What type is the XT-32 prim? Answer An RTX `OmniLidar`.

pages.text: Module 3 — Synthetic Data Generation (project) # Project goal: generate a randomized, labelled pallet-jack detection dataset (KITTI format) that a detector can be trained on. Lesson Video Diagram Script Generate a dataset with Replicator ▶ 3 pipeline m3_palletjack_sdg.py Project milestones # [ ] m3_palletjack_sdg.py --headless --test passes (5 different frames, palletjack-only labels) [ ] 20 frames generated with a window; you inspected images and labels [ ] Optional larger datasets, after the image/label checks: --num_frames 2000 --distractors warehouse and --num_frames 1000 --distractors None [ ] (outside Isaac Sim) detector trained with the course repo's notebook Before scaling up: overlay KITTI boxes on a few RGB images and explain any empty labels, poor visibility, or unexpected class assignments. Keep a bright and a dark example in your notes. Stretch project: add a second object class and compare two small datasets with one randomization setting changed. Do not treat the five-frame smoke test as evidence of real-world detector accuracy. You can now create inputs for perception experiments. Module 4 returns to robot control and shows how to exchange commands and sensor data with external software.

pages.title: 3 Generate a dataset
pages.text: Module 3: Synthetic Data Generation with Replicator (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course pages: Synthetic Data Generation for Perception Model Training in Isaac Sim Course lesson Version-specific? Where 1. Perception Models in Dynamic Robotic Tasks no (concepts) course site 2. What Is Synthetic Data Generation? no course site 3. Domain Randomization With Replicator no (concepts: object / lighting / texture randomization, the sim-to-real gap) course site 4. Generating a Synthetic Dataset Using Replicator yes this page 5. Fine-Tuning and Validating an AI Perception Model no (runs outside Isaac Sim, in TAO/PyTorch on the KITTI output) course repo local/ notebooks Goal: generate a KITTI-format dataset of pallet jacks in a warehouse, with randomized camera, poses, colors, lights, floor/wall textures and distractor objects. Your mission: make five images, inspect what changed, and decide whether their labels are usable before creating a larger dataset. Generating files is the first checkpoint; judging the data is the learning task. Script: scripts/m3_palletjack_sdg.py , a 6.1 port of the course's standalone_palletjack_sdg.py Expected result: --headless --test writes 5 different frames whose KITTI labels contain only palletjack (in learning_resource/output/palletjack_data/warehouse/Camera/ ). 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 1 h (+ generation time) · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Explain domain randomization and the sim-to-real gap Drive Replicator with the functional API (the 6.1 pattern) Produce and inspect a KITTI detection dataset Pallet-jack dataset pipeline (6.1) — interactive HTML Concepts # Why synthetic data? The simulator can generate annotations along with the rendered images, reducing manual labelling. You still need to inspect class assignments, bounding boxes, and visibility. Automatic annotation does not remove the need for dataset quality checks. Domain randomization. Vary camera pose, lighting, textures, and distractors to discourage reliance on accidental visual cues such as one background or one colour. This aims to improve robustness; it does not guarantee transfer to real images. Two gaps to consider: appearance (rendering realism) and content (scene variety). Replicator, two styles. Graph style ( with rep.trigger.on_frame(): rep.modify.pose(...) ) builds an OmniGraph that runs inside the orchestrator. Functional style ( rep.functional.modify.pose(prim, ...) ) changes the stage immediately in Python, then rep.orchestrator.step() renders and writes one frame. On this 6.1 build the functional style was the reliable one. Writers and annotators. Annotators compute per-frame data (rgb, bounding boxes, segmentation); writers (KittiWriter, BasicWriter, …) save annotator outputs in a dataset format. Part 1: Run the generator # The course clones a repo and edits generate_data.sh to point at Isaac Sim. With 6.1 you can run the ported script directly: cd ~/isaacsim # your Isaac Sim installation folder (contains isaac-sim.sh and python.sh) # quick look with a window, 20 frames ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m3_palletjack_sdg.py --num_frames 20 # two supported dataset variants; inspect a small sample before these longer runs ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m3_palletjack_sdg.py --headless --num_frames 2000 --distractors warehouse ./python.sh learning_resource/scripts/m3_palletjack_sdg.py --headless --num_frames 1000 --distractors None Options: --height 544 --width 960 (course defaults), --num_frames , --distractors warehouse|None , --data_dir , --rt_subframes (raise it if moving objects leave ghost trails). The first run downloads the warehouse and pallet jacks from NVIDIA's asset server and compiles shaders, so it's slow (minutes). Later runs are much faster. The course's --distractors additional set (hospital and office props) isn't included, because those asset paths moved between versions. Add your own with rep.create.from_usd(...) . Part 2: What the script does (and what changed) # The randomizations are the course's , with the same ranges: camera anywhere in the warehouse looking at the centre, pallet jack colours and poses (×6, scale 0.01), distractor poses, RectLight colour/intensity/ visibility, and floor/wall textures. How they are applied changed: Step Course (4.2/4.5) 6.1 Start app from omni.isaac.kit import SimulationApp , renderer: "RayTracedLighting" from isaacsim import SimulationApp , renderer: "RealTimePathTracing" Asset root omni.isaac.core.utils.nucleus.get_assets_root_path isaacsim.storage.native.get_assets_root_path (→ …/Assets/Isaac/6.1 ) Open warehouse omni.isaac.core.utils.stage.open_stage omni.usd.get_context().open_stage Add pallet jacks / distractors rep.create.from_usd(url, semantics=…, count=2) (graph API) rep.functional.create.reference(usd_path=url, semantics={"class": "palletjack"}) Randomize with rep.trigger.on_frame(num_frames=N): rep.modify.pose(…) , rep.randomizer.color(…) , rep.create.material_omnipbr(…) 🔄 a plain Python randomize() that calls rep.functional.modify.pose / attribute / visibility with NumPy random numbers Run rep.orchestrator.run() + wait loops 🔄 for i in range(N): randomize(); rep.orchestrator.step(rt_subframes=4) Only label pallet jacks custom update_semantics() : prim.RemoveProperty() on every non-palletjack pxr.Semantics label 🔄 the warehouse labels come from referenced layers, which RemoveProperty can't delete, so the script blocks them ( attr.Block() ), labels the pallet jacks with rep.functional.modify.semantics , and drops leftover Unlabelled rows from the KITTI files ( KittiWriter(semantic_filter_predicate=…) isn't applied by its fast bbox annotators in this build) Why the functional API? It's the pattern the 6.1 SDG examples use ( sdg_ur10_palletizing.py , randomizing_textures.py ), and the graph pattern misbehaved on this 6.1 build: rep.create.material_omnipbr + rep.randomizer.materials inside the trigger hung for more than 10 minutes ; graph randomizers driven by rep.orchestrator.step() fired only on the first frame , so every image was the same. ( on_frame(max_execs=N) + rep.orchestrator.run_until_complete() does still randomize every frame. That's the closest equivalent to the course's orchestrator.run() , if you want to keep graph randomizers.) Part 3: Output # learning_resource/output/palletjack_data/<warehouse|None>/ ├── metadata.txt └── Camera/ ├── rgb/ ← training images (0.png, 1.png, …) ├── object_detection/ ← KITTI labels, one .txt per image ("palletjack 0.00 0 0.00 x1 y1 x2 y2 …") └── depth/ semantic/ semantic_segmentation/ instance_segmentation/ (extra annotators) Look at a few images and label files, and check that each box surrounds a pallet jack. Many images are dark : that's the course's lighting randomization (each warehouse light is on only 1 time in 7). Lower the 7 in randomize() if you want brighter data. A sample from the actual run # Unmodified RGB output from Isaac Sim 6.1, seed 42, frame 0. The label file contains two pallet-jack boxes. Notice the partial object at the upper right: inspect the labels as well as the most obvious red object. A five-frame run with seed 42 gives five different images and only palletjack labels, but also one almost-black frame (mean RGB ≈ 5/255), one overexposed frame (≈ 253/255), and one frame with no labelled detections. Passing the smoke test does not make the data ready for training — review lighting, visibility and camera framing before a long run. Inspect before scaling up # Choose one bright frame, one dark frame, and one with an object partly hidden. Draw the KITTI boxes on each image (fields 5–8 are x1, y1, x2, y2 , using one-based field numbering). Check that the class is correct, coordinates are within the image, and the boxes match the intended objects. Keep images with no detections visible in your review too: an empty label file deserves inspection. Predict and compare: change one lighting parameter, generate another small sample, and explain what became easier or harder to see. Keep the seed and other settings fixed for the comparison. Decide what variation your intended camera actually needs before increasing the frame count. Part 4: Semantic labels in the GUI (optional part of the lesson) # 🔄 Tools > Replicator > Semantics Schema Editor (4.2: enable it under Window > Extensions). Selected objects : set Type class , Data = your label. Prim names : generate labels from prim names, stripping prefixes like SM_ / SK_ . In code (6.1): python import omni.replicator.core as rep rep.functional.modify.semantics(prim, {"class": "avocado"}, mode="add") # new functional API # graph API (still works inside rep.trigger blocks): rep.modify.semantics([("class", "avocado")]) Filters: class:vehicle|person (either), !class:sports_car (exclude). Part 5: Train / validate (course lesson 5) # This part runs outside Isaac Sim , so nothing changes for 6.1. Use the KITTI folders above as the dataset in the course repo's notebook ( synthetic_data_generation_training_workflow/local/ ). Going further in 6.1 # standalone_examples/api/isaacsim.replicator.examples/ has the current recommended patterns: sdg_getting_started_01…05.py (writers, annotators, functional API), randomizing_textures.py , randomizing_light_sources.py , simready_assets_sdg.py , cosmos_writer_simple.py . Check your result # Do this You should see m3_palletjack_sdg.py --headless --test PASS: randomized, palletjack-only KITTI data Camera/rgb/*.png different viewpoints, pallet jacks in varying colours/poses Camera/object_detection/*.txt only palletjack rows Exercises # Add a DomeLight with random intensity so fewer frames are dark. Add a second class ( class: cone on the traffic cones) and keep both classes in the labels. Write a 10-line script that draws the KITTI boxes on rgb/0.png to check them visually. Quiz # Why randomize the floor texture when we only care about pallet jacks? Answer To discourage dependence on one background. Test whether it helps on held-out images; randomization alone does not guarantee robustness. What does rep.orchestrator.step() do? Answer Renders one frame and lets attached writers save it. Why did the course's update_semantics() not remove the warehouse labels in 6.1? Answer They come from referenced layers; RemoveProperty can't delete those — the script blocks them.

pages.title: Module 4 project
pages.text: Module 4 — Developing Robots With Software-in-the-Loop (project) # Project goal: drive Nova Carter from ROS 2 ( /cmd_vel ), script scenes in Python, and stream its camera to an Isaac ROS pipeline. # Lesson Video Diagram Checkpoint 4.1 OmniGraph + /cmd_vel ▶ 4.1 control loop m4_nova_carter_cmd_vel.py 4.2 Python scripting ▶ 4.2 API layers m4_run_snippet.py + snippets 4.3 Camera images for Isaac ROS ▶ 4.3 SIL setup — The concept lessons ( Intelligent Robots , Software-in-the-Loop , Foundations of Image Segmentation ) are version-independent — read them on the course site. Project milestones # [ ] ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel … and teleop_twist_keyboard drive Nova Carter (4.1) — checkpoint passes [ ] Both Script Editor snippets run; the core-API one is in your own words (4.2) [ ] /rgb from the Hawk camera visible in rqt_image_view (4.3) Stretch project: combine 4.1 and 1.4 — write an rclpy node that reads /scan from Nova Carter's front RPLidar and publishes /cmd_vel to stop before obstacles. Optional capstone brief: stop before an obstacle # Combine the lidar and velocity-command lessons into one behavior. Start by identifying the actual scan topic on your scene and checking its frame and forward direction. Write a ROS 2 node that reads valid forward ranges and commands a stop below a distance you choose. Work through three milestones: Print the forward distance while the robot stays still. Compare it with a known obstacle placement. Publish zero velocity when the obstacle is too close, or when the scan is missing or stale. Test slow forward motion toward an obstacle and show the resulting stop. Repeat from another starting distance and record the smallest clearance. Done means: you can show a scan, a command, and the resulting motion; explain your threshold; and reproduce the stop. This is an extension brief, not an implemented or validated collision-avoidance controller. The course checkpoint only tests following velocity commands. Module 5 explores moving the robot-software side onto a Jetson.

pages.title: 4.1 Driving from /cmd_vel
pages.text: Lesson 4.1: Using OmniGraph to Drive a Robot from ROS 2 (Isaac Sim 6.1) # Course page: Developing Robots With SIL → Using OmniGraph to Drive a Robot in Isaac Sim ( …/developing-robots-with-sil-in-isaac-sim/03-using-omnigraph-to-drive-a-robot-in-isaac-sim.html ) The concept lessons before it ( Intelligent Robots , Software-in-the-Loop ) apply to any version. Read them on the course site. Goal: Nova Carter in the Simple Room, driven by ROS 2 geometry_msgs/Twist messages on /cmd_vel (from ros2 topic pub or teleop_twist_keyboard ). Checkpoint script: scripts/m4_nova_carter_cmd_vel.py Expected result: publishing linear.x = 0.5 on /cmd_vel moves Nova Carter more than 1 m in about 3.5 s (the checkpoint publishes real ROS 2 messages and checks this). 🎬 Narrated walkthrough · lesson ⏱ 45 min · caption text (.srt) · download .mp4 You will learn to Build a ROS 2 subscriber Action Graph by hand Drive a simulated robot from standard ROS tools ( ros2 topic pub , teleop) Explain software-in-the-loop (SIL) Driving Nova Carter from /cmd_vel — interactive HTML Concepts # Software-in-the-loop. The robot software runs unchanged; only its inputs (sensors) and outputs (actuators) are connected to a simulator instead of hardware. /cmd_vel ( geometry_msgs/Twist ) is the standard ROS interface for "drive with this velocity", so anything that drives a real mobile base (teleop, Nav2, your planner) can drive the simulated one. Twist. linear.x = forward m/s, angular.z = yaw rate rad/s; the other four fields are unused for a differential-drive robot — hence the two Break 3-Vector nodes picking x and z . Part 1: Scene # ./isaac-sim.sh → File > New . 🔄 Environment: Create > Environments > Simple Room (or Window > Browsers > Isaac Sim Assets → Environments → simple_room.usd → right-click → Add at current selection ). Zero its Translate. 🔄 Robot: Create > Robots > Nova Carter with Sensors . Move it next to the table and raise it slightly. Play and check it drops onto the floor. Stop . Part 2: Action Graph # Right-click nova_carter → Create > Visual Scripting > Action Graph , then open it ( Window > Graph Editors > Action Graph , or right-click the graph → Open Graph ). Add these nodes (search box in the graph editor; ROS nodes are in the Isaac Ros2 category): Node 6.1 type id On Playback Tick omni.graph.action.OnPlaybackTick ROS2 Context isaacsim.ros2.bridge.ROS2Context ROS2 Subscribe Twist isaacsim.ros2.bridge.ROS2SubscribeTwist Scale To/From Stage Units isaacsim.core.nodes.OgnIsaacScaleToFromStageUnit (optional, stage is already in metres) Break 3-Vector ×2 omni.graph.nodes.BreakVector3 Differential Controller isaacsim.robot.wheeled_robots.DifferentialController Articulation Controller isaacsim.core.nodes.IsaacArticulationController Make Array + Constant Token ×2 joint names (or type them straight into the Articulation Controller's jointNames ) Wire it up.
